en: Thinking this, brave Seytek
Took the inherited white saddle, saying,
“Let the hero saddle up and ride;
If a mighty challenger comes,
If a foe comes who can uproot mountains,
Let him enter battle without retreating;
Let him drive out his enemy’s soul
And rout them all together;
May it never chafe his back,
Nor trouble the heart of its rider;
Though he journey for six months,
Though he ride the horse hard and long,
Though he travel day and night,
Let him not falter when battle begins;
This white saddle was specially made
So it would not press the horse’s flanks.
May those who come after Bölökbay
Know his meticulous skill;
When they remember him in desperate straits,
May they think of us.”
The White Saddle, fashioned with such care,
Was set upon Kulansur,
But the dear lion, proud as a cock,
The valiant hero, did not stir.
The lady took his hand and embraced him,
And softly spoke:
“What fate awaits him?”
He lay back without stirring,
Revealing himself a lion among lions;
The dark-blue warrior took no heed,
But rejoiced at the thought of death.
Akjoltoy, son of Kutubiy,
Whose valor equaled countless troops,
Whose figure led the vanguard,
Whose presence loomed in peril,
Whose path was blessed when he went ahead,
Who, when an implacable foe came
And threatened his entrusted life,
Alone was equal to countless troops,
Mounted a horse like Kulansur,
Put on his coat of tempered iron,
Prepared his arms and took his spear,
And girded on his naked sword.
Tall and broad-shouldered,
He took a spear without a tassel,
Turned its point and hastened
To brave Seytek’s palace,
To Perizada’s fortress;
Gray-maned Joltoy now arrived.
At Akbermet’s palace,
Before it stood a painted hitching post,
And ten champions guarded the court;
What a wondrous host to behold!
Dark-eyed and radiant,
With sable fringe and broad hair ornaments,
Graceful beauties,
With shining camel-calf eyes,
With words sweeter than sugar,
Waists like sheaths and faces like the moon,
Serene beauties,
Whose sight gladdened the heart,
Serene and radiant women,
Who entered the house with stately grace,
True companions to heroes,
Who understood their inmost secrets:
The forty brides appointed for ceremony
Saw Akjoltoy
And darted forward like does,
Showing all the skill
Of those precious, luckless women;
They streamed forth like arrows,
And now took Joltoy’s horse,
Helping the fortunate champion
Down from his tall mount.
The white reins braided by forty companions
Were drawn from Joltoy’s hand,
And tied to the five-sided painted post,
Inlaid with precious stones,
Its every side
Encrusted with pure gold,
While its lower part
Was sheathed entirely in silver.
When this post was planted,
An immense part of the hero’s treasury
Was spent upon it.
Akbermet’s forty brides
Tied the horse with jingling ornaments,
Their nimbleness beyond compare,
Swiftly fastening it with a clatter.
Their splendor surpassed all others;
Fragrant perfume billowed from them,
They spoke serenely without laughter,
And the brides smiled;
The mortal soul of anyone
Who beheld them trembled.
With matchless agility,
They now drew open the door.
After Akjoltoy entered,
The forty nimble brides
Bustled about observing every custom,
Set down slabs of rich mutton,
And from potent black liquor
Poured a brimming ox-head bowl
Until its surface stood still.
The forty brides laughed in a row
And, approaching dear Uncle Joltoy
With graceful steps, offered it to him.
They also offered him
Fresh yellow foaming kumis.
When brave Joltoy drank it,
He readied himself like a hawk,
And from dear Joltoy’s lips
Came wisdom as if from the unseen.
His eyes could see afar;
Wise gray-maned Joltoy
Spoke slowly and with gravity:
“Oh, my child Akbermet,
If the famous rumor is true,
If it is sound and not a lie,
I have heard word from those who came
That your proud gray-maned champion
Has had a dream.
I have come and seen how you fare;
My child, let us interpret the dream you told.
My child, if a black golden eagle takes prey,
If a collared greyhound takes prey,
If it tracks across the black earth,
Then for the numberless Kyrgyz
Your noble gray-maned Seytek
Has become a stout house with walls
Through which no storm or wind can pass;
My child, he has become the ruin of the enemy he marked.
For the sons of the white-capped Kyrgyz,
My child, your prince Seytek has become khan.
Guarding the court and ruling the people,
He shall possess broad lands.
My child, if a black eagle takes prey,
If poison flows from its claws
And whatever it seizes dies,
Then, breaking treasuries and taking livestock,
Your prince shall become renowned.
A dark-blue son greater than himself,
Dark-bellied and blue-backed,
Who stirs conflict among the nations,
Who breaks through mountains to make roads,
Whoever dares resist,
He drives before him and disgraces,
Who brandishes a steel spear
And jostles the whole wide world—
Such a son shall be born to him.
He will subdue the Muslims who can speak
By the power of his tongue,
And drive the speechless fools before him
Until they beg for mercy.
He will wield a spear of steel,
And bring down whomever he marks,
Set the grassy steppe ablaze,
And burn his vengeful foes;
His fortune shall never leave his door.
My child, Bermet, when you give birth,
Bound in destiny to your hero,
A tiger will come into the world.
A hero named Kenen, lion-like,
Will indeed be born.
No enemy can breach his steel gate;
To all the peoples of the world, brave Kenen—
You shall indeed bear such a son.
Your camp shall settle upon the terrace;
My dear child Akbermet,
You shall crave the flesh of a lion.
Fierce and raging like a lion,
Breaking mountains to make roads,
Subduing the whole wide world—
Such a son shall indeed be yours.
At his feast we shall slaughter ninety head;
My child, we shall name him Kenen.
This is God’s gift,
The advent of true good fortune.
If he guards Ala-Too as his land,
If he makes his home by the White River,
Then Ala-Too, his homeland,
Shall indeed become his refuge.
If he takes the moon in his right hand,
And, when aroused, takes the sun,
Putting the Sun in the Moon’s place
And the Moon in the Sun’s place,
Then against the infidel rabble
We shall indeed wage battle.
Among all mortal sons,
Brave Seytek shall be a champion,
And we shall indeed join combat.
We shall take fully half
Of the Chinese lands.
For our forefathers who have passed,
My dear child Akbermet,
We shall indeed exact vengeance.
Stirring strife in Chin-Machin,
We shall ride out alongside him.
If all our enemy armies come,
If our resentful challengers come,
We shall extinguish the fires they kindled
And drive every one of them away;
The ranks arrayed against us—
When they clash, mortals will weary—
Of the immeasurable enemy
We shall indeed break the frontier.
My child, those foes who come from afar—
We shall indeed confound their boasts.
This is how I interpret your dream;
May the dream not come true, but good fortune come instead.
My dear child Akbermet,
But after that, our dream
Foretells a grievous trial.
If it settles in the east,
If, leaving not a blade among the gray grass,
It grazes across the face of the earth—
What is here today is gone tomorrow;
This deceitful world is filth.
Your dream is a grave portent:
If two swords are girded,
If they shatter stone at its solid heart,
And do not glance aside from the stone,
If a ravening dragon comes
And, when the dragon is struck,
The sword breaks in two,
Then across the face of the earth
The dragon’s wrath will pour down,
A calamitous affliction will arise
And leave us wretched.
That accursed creature, fit to be struck down,
Will grieve us with broken wings
And indeed bring us ruin!”
So saying, Akjoltoy
Reviled the ending of the dream
And fell silent as though he had drunk poison.
As Joltoy stood there,
His messenger Kadike,
A champion among the herdsmen,
Came rushing in with an uproar,
Bringing news:
“Hero, at Kichi-Chychkan and Chong-Chychkan,
In the valley of broad Talas,
Are a hundred men looming like mountains,
Strange in appearance and mighty in wrath.
They are not of our Kyrgyz people;
Those black-hearted curs,
Their conduct is far from ordinary.
They are not of our people’s stock;
Their horses have mattock-like hooves and broad rumps,
Chargers bred upon spacious lands,
Not horses from our country.
